html:
The Omaha are a Native American people of the Missouri River in northeastern Nebraska. They speak a Dhegiha Siouan language shared with the Ponca, Kaw, Osage and Quapaw, and by tradition came west from the Ohio valley.

They settled on the Missouri by the early 1700s, living in earth lodge villages, farming maize and hunting bison on the plains. Under the chief Blackbird they controlled river trade in the late 1700s. Smallpox struck in 1800 and 1801, killing many, Blackbird among them, and raids by the Lakota pressed them hard.

In 1854 they sold most of their land and kept a reservation in Nebraska, where the tribe lives today. The city of Omaha, founded that year, took their name. Susan La Flesche Picotte, an Omaha, became the first Native American woman to qualify as a doctor in 1889.
